questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: Ram writes a letter.

options.option_text: A letter is wrote by Ram
A letter is written by Ram
A letter was written by Ram
A letter has written by Ram

questions.explanation: Simple present active → 'is/are + V3' passive. Object 'a letter' → subject; subject 'Ram' → 'by Ram'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: They are painting the wall.

options.option_text: The wall is painted by them
The wall is being painted by them
The wall was being painted by them
The wall has been painted by them

questions.explanation: Present continuous active ('are painting') → 'is/are being + V3' passive.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: She has finished the report.

options.option_text: The report is finished by her
The report has been finished by her
The report was finished by her
The report had been finished by her

questions.explanation: Present perfect active ('has finished') → 'has/have been + V3' passive.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: Open the door.

options.option_text: The door is opened
Let the door be opened
The door was opened
The door has been opened

questions.explanation: Imperative → 'Let + object + be + V3' passive. Covers commands like 'shut the gate' → 'Let the gate be shut'.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: Who taught you French?

options.option_text: By whom were you taught French?
By who was French taught you?
Whom taught French to you?
Who was French taught by?

questions.explanation: Who → By whom (preposition + object form). Auxiliary before subject for interrogative: 'were you taught…'. Main verb 'teach' → 'taught' (V3).
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: They will announce the results tomorrow.

options.option_text: The results will announced tomorrow
The results will be announced tomorrow
The results are announced tomorrow
The results would be announced tomorrow

questions.explanation: Simple future active → 'will/shall be + V3' passive. Agent 'they' can be dropped when unimportant.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: The boy must finish the task.

options.option_text: The task must finished by the boy
The task must be finished by the boy
The task has been finished by the boy
The task was finished by the boy

questions.explanation: Modal + bare infinitive active ('must finish') → 'modal + be + V3' passive. Same for can/could/should/may/might/ought to.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: Choose the correct passive: She gave him a book.

options.option_text: He was given a book by her
He had been given a book by her
He has given a book by her
He was gave a book by her

questions.explanation: Two objects (he + book). Either can become the subject of the passive. The indirect-object option 'He was given a book by her' is usually preferred in exam keys. 'A book was given to him by her' is also valid but usually not the keyed form.
questions.subject: English

questions.stem: An artist painted this beautiful mural on the station wall. Which of the following is the correct passive voice form?

options.option_text: This beautiful mural is painted on the station wall by an artist
This beautiful mural was painted on the station wall by an artist
This beautiful mural has been painted on the station wall by an artist
This beautiful mural will be painted on the station wall by an artist

questions.explanation: B is correct because the original verb 'painted' is simple past tense, so the passive must use 'was/were + past participle' → 'was painted'. Option A wrongly uses simple present 'is painted'. Option C uses present perfect 'has been painted', and D uses future tense — both are tense mismatches with the original 'painted'.

questions.stem: Prizes were distributed to the winners by the Chief Guest. Which of the following correctly converts this sentence into active voice?

options.option_text: The winners distributed prizes to the Chief Guest
The Chief Guest distributed prizes to the winners
The Chief Guest will distribute prizes to the winners
Prizes are distributed to the winners by the Chief Guest

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'by the Chief Guest' identifies the doer → subject; 'winners' become the indirect object. The past tense 'were distributed' maps to simple past 'distributed'. Option A commits a classic inversion error — making the recipients ('winners') the active subject doing the distributing. Option C wrongly shifts tense to future. Option D retains passive structure (present tense).

questions.stem: You cannot use mobile phones inside the examination hall. Which of the following is the grammatically correct passive voice form?

options.option_text: Mobile phones can be used inside the examination hall
Mobile phones could not be used inside the examination hall
Mobile phones cannot be used inside the examination hall
Mobile phones are not to use inside the examination hall

questions.explanation: C is correct: modal passive of 'cannot use' is 'cannot be used' — the modal and negation both transfer intact. Option A is the most tempting distractor because it correctly forms the passive but drops the negation 'not', reversing the sentence's meaning. Option B wrongly changes 'cannot' (present) to 'could not' (past/conditional). Option D uses 'are not to use' which requires 'to be used' to form a valid passive infinitive construction.

questions.stem: Do not park vehicles near the emergency exit. Identify the correct passive voice form of this imperative sentence.

options.option_text: Vehicles should not park near the emergency exit
Let vehicles not be parked near the emergency exit
Vehicles were not parked near the emergency exit
The emergency exit must not have vehicles parked

questions.explanation: B is correct: the standard passive of a negative imperative ('Do not + V + object') follows the pattern 'Let + object + not + be + past participle'. So 'Do not park vehicles' → 'Let vehicles not be parked'. Option A uses a modal active construction ('should not park') — still active voice and merely advisory. Option C wrongly converts it to simple past declarative. Option D is an awkward restructuring that is grammatically non-standard.

questions.stem: The engineers had inspected the dam before the monsoon season began. Choose the correct passive voice form.

options.option_text: The dam has been inspected by the engineers before the monsoon season
The dam was being inspected by the engineers before the monsoon season
The dam had been inspected by the engineers before the monsoon season began
The dam will have been inspected by the engineers before the monsoon

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'had inspected' is past perfect active; its passive is 'had been inspected' — the auxiliary 'had' is retained, and 'been' is inserted before the past participle. The subordinate time clause 'before the monsoon season began' is carried over unchanged. Option A uses present perfect 'has been inspected', losing the past perfect. Option B uses past continuous passive 'was being inspected', a different tense entirely. Option D uses future perfect, which is contradicted by the context.

questions.stem: A reporter was interviewing the minister when the fire broke out. Which of the following correctly rewrites the main clause in passive voice?

options.option_text: The minister was interviewed by a reporter when the fire broke out
The minister was being interviewed by a reporter when the fire broke out
The minister had been interviewed by a reporter when the fire broke out
The minister is being interviewed by a reporter when the fire broke out

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'was interviewing' is past continuous active; its passive form is 'was being + past participle' → 'was being interviewed'. The ongoing action at the moment of interruption ('when the fire broke out') demands past continuous, not simple past. Option A ('was interviewed') is simple past passive — it loses the continuous/ongoing aspect and implies the interview was completed, which contradicts the simultaneity with the fire. Option C uses past perfect passive, implying the interview preceded the fire. Option D uses present continuous, creating a tense clash with 'broke out'.

questions.stem: The administration could have prevented the flood damage with timely action. Which passive transformation is grammatically correct?

options.option_text: The flood damage could have been prevented by the administration with timely action
The flood damage could be prevented by the administration with timely action
The flood damage could have been preventing by the administration with timely action
The flood damage could have prevented by the administration with timely action

questions.explanation: A is correct: the active modal perfect 'could have prevented' converts to passive as 'could have been prevented' — modal + have + been + past participle. Option B ('could be prevented') drops 'have', turning a past hypothetical into a general present possibility — a meaning change. Option C uses the present participle 'preventing' instead of the past participle 'prevented', which is a structural error (passive requires past participle). Option D omits 'been', producing 'could have prevented' — which is still active voice in form and syntactically incomplete as a passive.
